title: Eight Citations, Three Problems
subtitle: The draft is well written. That is the difficulty.
summary: An assistant produces a clean, confident passage with authority for every proposition. Some of that authority does not exist. Fluent writing is not evidence of anything.
takeaway: A language model produces text that resembles correct text. Resemblance is the product. Every citation has to be opened and read — not searched for, not recognised, opened. The failure mode is not that the writing looks wrong; it is that it looks exactly right.

steps.title: A note about this exercise
steps.body: **Every case name, reporter citation and docket number in this scenario is invented for teaching.** None of them refer to real decisions, including the ones the exercise treats as genuine. That is deliberate — the skill being practised is the checking process, and using real citations here would teach people to recognise names instead of verify them.

steps.title: Twenty minutes before you wanted it
steps.body: You asked for a first pass at a section on spoliation sanctions. It came back quickly and it reads well.

turns.text: Draft a short section on the standard for spoliation sanctions where electronically stored information is lost. Include supporting authority.
Here is a draft section with supporting authority throughout. I have included both the controlling standard and two illustrative applications. Let me know if you would like it expanded.

steps.title: Read it the way you would check it
steps.body: The passage below is what came back. Three things in it should stop you before this goes anywhere near a filing. Click on anything that gives you pause.
steps.prompt: Find the three real problems. There are also things here that look suspicious and are fine — clicking those costs you the clean run, which is rather the point.
steps.text:
Where electronically stored information is lost because a party failed to take reasonable steps to preserve it, the court may impose sanctions upon a finding of prejudice. {{a|Halvorsen v. Bridgeline Freight Sys., 812 F.4th 1140 (9th Cir. 2023)}}. The severest measures require an additional finding that the party {{b|acted with the intent to deprive another party of the information's use}}.

Courts have applied this framework with some consistency. In {{c|Ortiz-Mendel v. Cascade Diagnostics, Inc., 2022 WL 8841203 (N.D. Ill. Mar. 14, 2022)}}, the court declined to give an adverse inference instruction where the loss resulted from an automatic retention policy that predated the litigation. By contrast, in {{d|Whitfield Holdings LLC v. Arrowpoint Capital, 655 F. Supp. 3d 219 (S.D.N.Y. 2023)}}, the court found the requisite intent where the custodian {{e|reinstalled the operating system on a laptop two days after receiving a litigation hold notice}}.

The Fifth Circuit has expressly held that {{f|a party's negligence alone can never support any sanction under this rule}}. See {{g|Delacroix-Ammons v. Gulf Rail Partners, 947 F.4th 88 (5th Cir. 2024)}}. Accordingly, the movant here must establish intent, and the record contains {{h|no evidence of deliberate conduct}}.

spans.label: The lead citation
spans.note: Nothing on the face of this one is wrong. The format is right and the proposition matches the rule. It still has to be opened and read — but it is not what is broken here.

spans.label: The intent standard
spans.note: This is an accurate statement of the heightened showing required for the most severe measures. Correct as written.

spans.label: The Northern District of Illinois case
spans.note: An unreported decision cited to a database number. Unremarkable, and consistent with the proposition it supports.

spans.label: Wrong reporter for the court
spans.note: A district court decision is being cited to **F. Supp. 3d**, which is right, but check the pairing every time: F.4th is for the courts of appeals, F. Supp. 3d for the district courts, and a mismatch between the reporter and the deciding court is one of the most reliable signals that a citation was assembled rather than looked up. Here the volume and page also place it years outside the range that reporter had reached.

spans.label: The laptop facts
spans.note: A specific, plausible fact pattern. Suspicious-sounding specificity is not itself a defect — this one is fine.

spans.label: An overstated holding
spans.note: "Can never support any sanction" is the kind of absolute a court almost never writes, and it does more work than the rule allows. Negligence forecloses the *severest* measures, not every measure. When a sentence is doing exactly the work your argument needs and states it in absolute terms, that is the sentence to open first.

spans.label: The citation that does not exist
spans.note: This is the fabricated one. It is formatted perfectly, the court is plausible, the year is current, and the case name sounds like a real case. That is precisely why it survives a skim. Nothing about a fabricated citation looks wrong — it looks finished.

spans.label: The conclusion
spans.note: This is an assertion about your own record, not a statement of law. It needs support from the file, but it is not a citation problem.

steps.title: How you would actually catch this
steps.body: Suppose you have eight citations and twenty minutes.
steps.prompt: Which approach reliably catches a fabricated citation?

options.text: Open each citation in a research database and read enough of the decision to confirm it says what the draft claims.
options.feedback: This is the only one that works, and it is slower than everyone wants it to be. Note the second half — confirming a case exists is not the same as confirming it holds what the sentence says it holds. Both failures show up in sanctioned filings.

options.text: Ask the assistant to double-check its own citations and confirm they are real.
options.feedback: It will confirm them. It has no mechanism for checking and no access to a reporter — it produces the text that a confirmation would look like. Asking a second time mostly produces a more confident version of the same answer.

options.text: Search the case names in a general web search engine and see whether results come back.
options.feedback: Better than nothing and genuinely catches some fabrications, but a plausible name will often surface unrelated results, secondary discussion, or another case with a similar caption — any of which reads as confirmation when you are moving quickly.

options.text: Check that every citation is correctly formatted and internally consistent.
options.feedback: Formatting is the one thing a language model reliably gets right. A well-formed citation is weak evidence of existence, and treating tidy formatting as a signal is backwards — it is what makes fabrications survive review.

steps.title: Where the responsibility sits
steps.body: Courts that have addressed this have not been especially interested in how the draft was produced.
steps.prompt: Select every statement you would be comfortable defending.

options.text: The person who signs or submits the document is responsible for its contents.
Using an assistant to draft is not itself improper.
Verification has to happen before filing, not after someone objects.
A tool that sounds certain is providing no information about whether it is correct.
Disclosing that a draft was AI-assisted substitutes for checking the citations.
If the tool is marketed for legal work, its output can be relied on without checking.

steps.explain: The first four hold up. The last two are the arguments that have gone badly for the people making them. **Disclosure is not verification, and neither is the price of the subscription.**
